extracted.intended_audience: legislators, tribunal designers, administrative law policymakers, and senior tribunal/agency officials responsible for designing or reforming social security/unemployment insurance appeal processes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed statutory/regulatory standards for organizing review tribunals, access to appeal, procedural formalities, tribunal composition, and the quality/timing/publication of tribunal decisions in the context of unemployment insurance and related federal social security litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal access to review
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of avenues of contentious review is meaningful only when all the parties who are equally affected by the procedure enjoy equal access to them, subject to minimal formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access must be available to all interested parties on equal terms (no distinctions based on union membership etc.). The report proposes amending sec.95 to give the same right of appeal to UIC, claimants, employers, unions and employers' associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal formalities for access
rubrics_metrics.description: Access depends on the ease with which the right to apply for review can be exercised and thus on the formalities with which the party applying for review is required to comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain minimal, liberal formal requirements (e.g., notices of appeal need only be in writing and include grounds). The Tribunal should adopt an attitude marked by as little formality as the UIC and may delegate form distribution to the UIC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical accessibility of hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Access has a spatial dimension — the choice of hearing location may pose obstacles to participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards should sit in locations other than the main centre when justified by outlying appeals; tribunals should sit as close as possible to claimant's home to minimize travel expenses and encourage participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and independence of tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: Review tribunals must be able, by virtue of their composition and operating procedures, to render decisions quickly and impartially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence includes sitting in neutral premises (not on administrative authority's premises), removing leave-to-appeal powers from authors of decisions, and constituting tribunals separate from the UIC (or equivalent administrative body).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and authoritativeness of decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of the tribunals should, because of their clarity, logic and legal soundness, be regarded as authoritative by the public and administrative authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should be written, contain statements of reasons, be sent to parties and interested persons, and be published regularly (or at least those that contribute to legal development). The Tribunal should supervise lower tribunals to improve quality and uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal rights of appeal regardless of union membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership in a union or an employers' association should not affect the extent of the right of appeal with respect to unemployment insurance benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 95 should be amended so that the Commission, claimants, employers, worker associations and employer associations all have the same right to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform leave-to-appeal regime (prefer upward equalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether rights of appeal should be equalized upwards (require leave for all) or downwards (relieve all of leave requirement); the report prefers the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A second level of appeal should be used only for important/difficult cases; leave criteria (importance/difficulty/special circumstances) are already specified for some appellants and should apply uniformly. When the board decision is unanimous, leave should be required for all appellants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who grants leave to appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave to appeal should be granted by the Tribunal before which a hearing is desired and not by the author of the decision in dispute (e.g., chairman of the Board).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfer power to grant leave from the chairman of the Board of referees to the Tribunal; the Tribunal (or its president) should decide on leave applications without a hearing and give reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural timing for leave and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Time-limits to expedite appeals: appeals to the higher tribunal shortened to 45 days; if prior leave required application for leave filed within 15 days; Tribunal to decide on application within the next 15 days so appellant still has 15 days to file notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave to appeal should be exercisable by the president (or vice-president) without hearing; decisions on leave should be given promptly and with reasons. These changes aim to cut down very slow current average (cited as 33 weeks to hearing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic formal requirements for appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals must be in writing and contain a statement of the grounds of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These basic requirements (from regs. 184(1) and (2)) should be transposed into the Act and preserved; beyond that, presentation may be liberal and forms may be provided by the UIC/registry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal responsibility to collect parties' comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The office of the Umpire (or successor Tribunal) should be given responsibility for collecting the comments of all the parties to the litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal could send a form designed for submitting comments at the same time as it notifies parties that an appeal has been filed, and include parties listed in relevant regulations and those recognized as having an interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral venue principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The desirability of the review tribunal sitting on the premises of the administrative authority whose decisions it reviews is questioned; hearings should be held in neutral locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards sitting in neutral public buildings rather than UIC premises would demonstrate independence; presence of clerks and files in the neutral building suffices to retain administrative advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and review of tripartite representation on Boards
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of representatives of employers and unions on Boards of referees is historically justified and fundamentally fair and should not be questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While keeping tripartite structure, consider improving chairman representation and recruitment to better reflect social realities and knowledge of local social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden consultation in appointing chairmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation prior to appointment of chairmen by the Governor in Council should have a broader ambit, including groups with local roots and expertise in social administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form and scope of consultation should be flexible to local conditions, aiming to secure chairmen with in‑depth social problem knowledge and good relationship with the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender representation on Boards
rubrics_metrics.description: When soliciting recommendations for appointments, ensure lists contain sufficient women candidates so that there will always be at least one woman on the Board when the appeal is filed by a woman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors practice elsewhere (e.g., Great Britain) and is desirable given the high proportion of female workers served by UIC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce participation (turn-taking) by panel representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels should systematically eliminate representatives of employers and unions who refuse, without overriding justification, to take their turn on the Board on more than three occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same standard should be applied to chairmen, though removal procedures may be more cumbersome; aim is to ensure fair rotation and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace part-time judicial Umpires with permanent specialized tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of overload, lack of specialized knowledge, slow procedure and lack of control over caseload/quality/publication, Umpires should be replaced by a new Federal Social Security Tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal would have jurisdiction over unemployment insurance and potentially all federal social security litigation; its composition and powers governed by special Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal jurisdiction and core powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal should have power to confirm, rescind or amend disputed decisions or refer the case back; to amend its own decisions; to decide on validity of direct interest of interveners; and to exercise leave-to-appeal powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers should be specified in statute and the Tribunal should determine general procedural framework and formalities (subject to Governor in Council approval of regulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal rulemaking and regulatory authority (92A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, make regulations concerning the quorum for a board of referees; practice and procedure before a board; formalities in respect of appeals and applications for leave; and formalities for observations/representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations would apply to appeals before both the Tribunal and the Board of referees and govern formalities for leaves and representations (transposing reg.184 into the Act as needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative supervision of lower tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal should exercise administrative supervision over the Boards: monitor adherence to rules, ensure uniformity, issue circulars and co‑ordination measures, and provide members with necessary training and documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal should be responsible for continuing education and for maintaining consistency in methods across Boards of referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and dissemination of caselaw
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal should be required by its enabling legislation to publish a collection of its decisions at regular intervals (or at least those decisions that contribute to evolution of the law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current slow and inadequate publication systems should be replaced; reg.186(2) to be repealed and publication duties statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal composition, appointment and term limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Members should be appointed by the Governor in Council; for unemployment insurance alone three members (including president) may suffice, but for broader jurisdiction 5–7 members recommended; members should hold office for a maximum period of five years (renewable) and no member should hold office for more than ten years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal needn't be entirely lawyers but should include some lawyers; avoid replicating tripartite structure at this level; require president (and possibly one or two others) to be lawyers; aim for cross-section of society and technical skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative staffing: Registry and Secretariat roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunal administrative staff should be divided: a Registry responsible for physical organisation, correspondence and processing appeal files; and a Secretariat responsible for supervising and coordinating Boards, training members and preparing caselaw reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibilities of these branches should be defined in the Tribunal's enabling Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-member hearings with discretion for benches
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the Tribunal would normally be heard by one member sitting alone, subject to a provision empowering the president to direct hearing by himself and two others for important or complex cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids tripartite benches at the higher level while preserving capacity for multi-member consideration when warranted by importance or complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to sit anywhere and informality rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Social Security Tribunal should be empowered to sit anywhere in Canada and the rule of informality (present sec.93(1)) should apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include power to sit anywhere in enabling Act and in the Acts providing appeal procedures to ensure public accessibility and procedural informality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to be heard and hearing application timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunal must grant any party having an interest a reasonable opportunity to submit representations; appellant, Commission or interested person may apply in writing for a hearing within fifteen days of docket filing and Tribunal shall grant a hearing; Tribunal may direct a hearing at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At least 14 days prior notice of hearing must be given to appellant, Commission, and other persons/associations with immediate interest; procedure at hearing determined by Tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written reasons and notification of decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision of the Tribunal shall be in writing and shall contain a statement of reasons, and a copy shall be sent to the appellant, the Commission, and any other person or association having an immediate interest in the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions (including leave decisions) should indicate grounds and be communicated to interested parties to support transparency and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspensive effect of appeals on benefit payments defined in statute
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where appeal has suspensive effect on payment of benefits, the relevant period should be defined by the Act; the 21-day period in sec.103(2)(a) should be reduced to 15 days to fit with the 15-day leave application timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where leave is required and given to UIC, the application for leave should be considered to have equivalent suspensive effect as an appeal filed as of right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review route for Tribunal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of the Tribunal, including those with regard to leave to appeal, should be subject to judicial review by the Federal Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose amending sec.100 to restrict judicial review avenue to the 'application to review and set aside' under sec.28 of the Federal Court Act, simplifying process and aligning with trend toward Federal Court of Appeal jurisdiction.
